clue.text: Excellent landlord begins a sentence

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: the thing that begins every sentence

parts.note: capital is an old-fashioned exclamation meaning excellent or first-rate
a letter is one who lets property, a landlord

explanation.surface: A splendid landlord opens proceedings with a sentence, perhaps at a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is read as one who lets, not a piece of mail; the definition describes what the answer does rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Every written sentence opens with an upper-case character, so this is a description of its job.

clue.text: Peacock's residence of some note

definitions.note: possessive standing for a title: the work belonging to Peacock

parts.note: a crotchet is a musical note, a quarter-note
a castle is a grand residence

explanation.surface: A bird's home is apparently rather a notable place.
explanation.walkthrough: Peacock is Thomas Love Peacock, the English satirical novelist, not the bird; one of his novels is titled after a fictional country house.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Love Peacock published this satirical novel in 1831, named after the house where its talkers gather.

clue.text: Master it, and you do your best

definitions.text: Master it, and you do your best

parts.words: Master it, and you do your best
parts.note: put 'master' in front of this word and you get a person's finest work, so adding it to master gives your best

explanation.surface: Encouragement to learn a skill thoroughly in order to perform well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' is not a verb here but a word to be prefixed: master plus the answer is a supreme achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: A masterpiece is the finest work an artist produces, so this short word completes that compound.

clue.text: It's presumably on the cards they act dishonourably

definitions.text: It's presumably on the cards they act dishonourably

parts.words: It's presumably on the cards they act dishonourably
parts.note: 'on the cards' means likely, but also hints at card tricks played by cheats and conjurors

explanation.surface: It is to be expected that certain people will behave badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the cards' looks like the idiom for 'likely', but it also points at people who do tricks with playing cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindlers and cheats who deceive others by trickery, including sleight of hand with cards.

clue.text: Hopeful signs when silver

parts.note: points to the proverb that every cloud has a silver one of these, a hopeful sign

explanation.surface: A description of something precious that offers optimism.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'every cloud has a silver lining' supplies the word; the plural matches 'signs'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright edges of a dark cloud stand in the proverb for hope within misfortune.

clue.text: A gentle way of being graceful

indicators.note: 'way' here means a manner or arrangement, so the letters of the phrase are laid out a new way

explanation.surface: Moving gently is a means of appearing graceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way' tells you to rearrange A GENTLE, giving the seven letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Refined and stylish in movement or appearance is to be graceful.

clue.text: Traders go to it when in need of change

definitions.text: Traders go to it when in need of change

parts.words: Traders go to it when in need of change
parts.note: shopkeepers open the cash drawer when they need coins to give a customer

explanation.surface: Merchants turn somewhere when they want things to be different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like reform or novelty but means coins handed back to a customer.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop's cash register or money drawer is where the coins are kept.

clue.text: He's a regular tell-tale

parts.note: 'tell-tale' usually means a sneak, but here it is someone who habitually tells tales, a storyteller

explanation.surface: A complaint about someone who always sneaks to the teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: A tell-tale is normally an informer; read literally it is one who tells tales, which is a practised storyteller.
explanation.definitionFit: A skilled anecdotist who entertains company with stories.

clue.text: Obey this direction, and you can't go wrong

definitions.text: Obey this direction, and you can't go wrong

parts.words: Obey this direction, and you can't go wrong
parts.note: an instruction to stay on one side, where 'can't go wrong' plays on right as the opposite of wrong

explanation.surface: Advice that following the rules always leads to good results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' is both a side of the road and the opposite of wrong, so following this sign keeps you from going wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A traffic instruction to stay on the starboard side of a road or path.

clue.text: Following the bidding

parts.note: 'bidding' looks like auction or bridge bids, but means doing what one is told

explanation.surface: Something that happens after the auction bids are in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bidding' suggests an auction or card game; read as a command, following it is compliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Compliance with orders: doing someone's bidding.

clue.text: The second of three sisters well-fed on treacle

definitions.text: The second of three sisters well-fed on treacle

parts.words: The second of three sisters well-fed on treacle
parts.note: in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Dormouse tells of three sisters living at the bottom of a treacle well

explanation.surface: A story about the middle girl of three who are fond of syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dormouse's tale in Lewis Carroll's book names Elsie, the answer and Tillie as the sisters in the treacle well; 'well-fed' hides 'well'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll named the second sister of the Dormouse's story with an anagram of Alice.

clue.text: It sounds an exclusive club

indicators.note: 'sounds' says the word we want is pronounced like another word

parts.note: a clique is an exclusive little group of people

explanation.surface: A private members' club is announced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exclusive club' reads as one phrase, but 'club' is the definition, a golf club, and 'an exclusive' gives the word heard.
explanation.definitionFit: An old Scottish golf club with an iron head, similar to a modern long iron.

clue.text: A tidy entry for the Cattle Show?

definitions.meaning: ... and orderly, a word meaning tidy
an archaic word for an ox or bovine animal, which could be entered at a show

explanation.surface: A neat exhibit is submitted to an agricultural show.
explanation.walkthrough: The old word for cattle (as in neatherd, neat's-foot oil) is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are real: tidy and orderly, and an old term for an ox or cow.

clue.text: Certainty of a little cut

definitions.meaning: in British slang a sure thing, especially a bet bound to win
a small cut made with scissors

explanation.surface: Being sure of a small trim at the barber's.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers a small scissor cut and, in British slang, a sure thing or easy win.

clue.text: It has a lasting effect

parts.note: a durable quality; also hints at the perm, a hairdo meant to last

explanation.surface: Something that leaves a long-lasting impression.
explanation.walkthrough: The quality of enduring is literally what has a lasting effect; a permanent wave is the hairdresser's lasting effect.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of lasting indefinitely without change.

clue.text: There are three in the realm

definitions.text: There are three in the realm

parts.words: There are three in the realm
parts.note: the traditional three divisions of the realm: Lords Spiritual, Lords Temporal and Commons

explanation.surface: A statement that a kingdom has three of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'three estates of the realm' are the traditional orders of society in Britain: clergy, nobility and commons.
explanation.definitionFit: The orders or classes of a kingdom's political body, traditionally three.

clue.text: A distinctive sign of good business

definitions.text: A distinctive sign of good business

parts.words: A distinctive sign of good business
parts.note: a sign or symbol distinctive of a firm, its registered brand

explanation.surface: An indicator that a company is doing well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign of good business' suggests success, but it is the brand mark that identifies a trader's goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A registered symbol or name that identifies a company's goods.

clue.text: Sounds like a couple of them added on

indicators.note: the phrase says the answer is pronounced like the words that follow

parts.note: a couple of them could be 'their two', two belonging to them

explanation.surface: Two items appended that make a noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Their two' spoken sounds like the answer, a formal word meaning in addition to that.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal adverb meaning in addition, attached or appended to the thing mentioned.

clue.text: Carried with acclaim

parts.note: a winner borne shoulder-high in triumph, as if seated on a chair; also hints at a meeting's motion being carried

explanation.surface: A motion is passed with enthusiastic approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried' suggests a motion passing a vote, but here it is a hero carried shoulder-high.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting a victor on supporters' shoulders, as if on a seat, in celebration.

clue.text: "All for your ——. We are not here" (M. N. Dream)

definitions.text: "All for your ——. We are not here" (M. N. Dream)

parts.words: "All for your ——. We are not here" (M. N. Dream)
parts.note: a line from Quince's mispunctuated prologue in A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 5

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Quince's prologue to the mechanicals' play garbles its punctuation; the missing word means pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: The word fills the line as the audience's pleasure or enjoyment.

clue.text: Greek governor for eleven months of the year?

definitions.meaning: the governor of a nome, a province of modern or ancient Greece or Egypt
the eleven months that are not the third month, read as 'no' plus that month

explanation.surface: A Greek official who works all year except one month.
explanation.walkthrough: The governor's title split as NO MARCH describes every month but one.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a Greek nome, an administrative department.

clue.text: A fresh drink in town

parts.note: fresh means new
port is a fortified wine, a drink

explanation.surface: A new beverage in a town.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in South Wales, among other places of the name.

clue.text: His looks don't belie him

parts.note: 'looks' read as what someone sees, so a person whose seeing is true to his name

explanation.surface: A man whose appearance matches his character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks' means appearance in the surface, but is read as acts of looking: a visionary's looks are his calling.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophet or visionary, literally one who sees.

clue.text: Not the match that suggests elopement

definitions.text: Not the match that suggests elopement

parts.words: Not the match that suggests elopement
parts.note: an elopement is a hasty marriage, so the match meant is the fuse that burns gradually

explanation.surface: A marriage that is not a hasty runaway affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks like a marriage, but a slow match is a fuse used to fire old guns; an elopement is a quick match.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow match is a slow-burning fuse cord; the word is the opposite of quick.

clue.text: You'll get the answer to this in no time

definitions.text: You'll get the answer to this in no time

parts.words: You'll get the answer to this in no time
parts.note: 'in no time' means quickly, but read literally the answer is the word for at no time

explanation.surface: An encouraging remark that this clue will be solved quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In no time' sounds like 'very soon'; read literally, the answer is the word meaning at no time.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb meaning at no time at all.

clue.text: Wordsworth's cuckoo might be called a wandering one

definitions.text: Wordsworth's cuckoo might be called a wandering one

parts.words: Wordsworth's cuckoo might be called a wandering one
parts.note: Wordsworth's poem To the Cuckoo asks whether to call it a bird or but a wandering sound

explanation.surface: A remark about how the poet described a migrating bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem's line is 'O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird, Or but a wandering ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cuckoo is heard far more than seen, so the poet calls it a sound wandering the valley.

clue.text: Cheshire centre for bargain-hunters?

definitions.meaning: a town in Cheshire, a county in north-west England, near Manchester
an event selling goods at reduced prices, sought by bargain-hunters

explanation.surface: A shopping centre in Cheshire for people seeking bargains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre' looks like a shopping centre but means a town: SALE is a town in Cheshire, a county of north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a Cheshire town and a period of reduced prices.

clue.text: Tropical plant found in the Italian Alps

indicators.note: 'found in' signals that the letters are sitting inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A tropical plant has turned up in the mountains of northern Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' points inside 'ItaLIAN Alps', where the letters run across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: A woody climbing vine of tropical rainforests.

clue.text: The outcome of a " down-to earth" policy?

definitions.text: The outcome of a " down-to earth" policy?

parts.words: The outcome of a " down-to earth" policy?
parts.note: 'down-to-earth' means practical, but read literally it means bringing things down to the ground

explanation.surface: Asks what results from a sensible, practical policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down-to-earth' suggests common sense; literally it is bringing aircraft or ships to the ground, or teaching basics thoroughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Running aground or keeping aircraft on the ground; also a thorough basic training.

clue.text: Directive with a sinister meaning

parts.note: 'sinister' is Latin and heraldry for the left-hand side, so the directive points that way

explanation.surface: An order with an ominous hidden purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinister' looks like menacing, but in Latin and heraldry it means on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: A road sign telling traffic to stay on the port side.
